lessons.title: What does it actually mean for something to be healthy?
lessons.sourceSections: Introduction; finite forest example, Section 5 and Appendix A
lessons.summary: Present condition, represented viable continuation capacity, and the role of declared scenario, time horizon, specification, and requirement.

lessons.title: What is a viable continuation?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper I, Sections 2–4; finite-forest candidate filter clarified in Paper IV
lessons.summary: The complete viable family, the separation of lawfulness and continuation, and capacity as an observer-dependent representation of viable histories.

lessons.title: Can two systems have different capacities but still be equally healthy?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper I, Sections 6–8; requirement-visible quotient and sufficiency
lessons.summary: Capacity sets can differ while agreeing on every declared adequacy question; the requirement-visible quotient records precisely those distinctions, with an explicit new-query boundary.

lessons.title: Why having the capacity to survive is not the same as being robust
lessons.sourceSections: Paper I Sections 9–11 and discussion of scientific scope: presentation invariance, positive persistence/robustness and observation sufficiency
lessons.summary: Success-only capacity may not determine robustness, present realization alone may not determine prospective Health, and observation/representation must preserve the distinctions its questions need.

lessons.title: How can the same system be healthy in one context and unhealthy in another?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper II, Sections 1 and 5–8: contextual licensing, developmental stage, stage-only class splitting and horizon change
lessons.summary: A contextual health judgment may change when the capacity changes or when the licensed requirement language changes, even with fixed capacity.

lessons.title: How can we carry information about health from one context to another?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper II, Sections 2–4 and 8–11: relational transport, determinacy, health-visible quotient and stage obstruction; external-support illustration in Section 12
lessons.summary: Raw target capacities can be indeterminate while a target adequacy class is determined. Stage-specific questions can obstruct transport, and determinacy alone does not preserve full Health.

lessons.title: Can a system be healthy if it depends on something outside itself to survive?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper II Section 12 and Section 7: open-system support states, horizon transport, withdrawal and comparison with the five-state forest
lessons.summary: The four-state open-system example proves that equal short-horizon capacities need not determine long-horizon capacity; withdrawal changes reserve-Health despite preserved present realization. It distinguishes formal dependence from empirical claims.

lessons.title: How do we know whether a measurement contains enough information to determine health?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper III Sections 1–5 and 9: representation sufficiency and principal refinement theorem; probability illustration from Section 12.3 and full thresholds from Section 10.1
lessons.summary: The principal theorem characterizes representations sufficient for a query family exactly as refinements of its query-visible quotient. Stipulated probability distributions illustrate why an accurate yes/no observation can be insufficient and why deterministic postprocessing cannot recover erased information.

lessons.title: Why more information can sometimes make prediction harder
lessons.sourceSections: Paper III Sections 6–8: source refinement, target coarsening, minimal sufficient target determinacy and exact Paper-II forest witness
lessons.summary: More source information preserves exact determinacy for a fixed target; finer target information imposes stronger exact demands. The canonical query-visible quotient is the coarsest sufficient target, and the finite forest witness separates raw-target failure from health-visible determination.

lessons.title: Is being able to survive the same as being likely to survive?
lessons.sourceSections: Paper III Sections 10.1–10.2 and 12.2–12.3: finite response probability-threshold queries and the attained all-budget minimum-cost code
lessons.summary: Theorems for complete bounded rational probability thresholds and fixed-atom all-budget cost queries identify exact task-visible statistics. Possibility, probability and affordability remain distinct.

lessons.title: Having a way to survive is not the same as being able to control your survival
lessons.sourceSections: Paper III Sections 11 and 12.1, 12.4: controlled responses and policy-robust recovery, route-summary representation, challenge profiles and failure-aware robust persistence
lessons.summary: Separates recovery possibility, controlled recovery, multiple routes, policy-level robustness and failure-aware robustness over a declared challenge family.

lessons.title: How information gets lost—and why it matters for health
lessons.sourcePaper: Information Provenance and Conservative Enrichment in Prospective Health
lessons.sourceSections: Paper IV Sections 3–8 and Theorems 7.1–7.2: complete five-state forest, candidate lawfulness filtering, detailed and simplified capacities, full Health-profile quotient and lost-versus-ignored distinctions
lessons.summary: The exact five-to-four-to-three class hierarchy records where different forest distinctions disappear: recovered/adapted at response projection versus baseline/recovered in the declared Health answer language.
